Learning Objectives
Review the morphologic changes characteristic of femoroacetabular impingement syndrome
and the manner in which to identify them radiographically.
Discuss the demographic groups commonly affected by femoroacetabular impingement.
Explain the typical symptoms of patients with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome and
physical examination maneuvers used to differentiate femoroacetabular impingement
syndrome from other conditions in the same region.
Review nonsurgical and surgical treatment strategies for femoroacetabular impingement
syndrome and common pitfalls/complications of hip arthroscopy.

Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) syndrome is recognized as a common cause of hip
dysfunction and secondary osteoarthritis.
In FAI syndrome, distinct morphologic abnormalities produce repetitive impingement between
the acetabulum and the femoral head-neck junction.

Overview
First described by Ganz et al,1,2 FAI syndrome is a pathologic condition resulting from
abnormal acetabular or femoral head/neck anatomy that has been implicated in
acetabular labral tearing, acetabular chondral injury, and eventually osteoarthritis. Three
types of FAI syndrome have been identified: cam, pincer, and combined cam/pincer.
Cam impingement is characterized by abnormalities that are femoral-based, such as
aspherical femoral head and reduced head-neck offset, and femoral
retroversion/relative retroversion that results in repetitive abutment of the acetabular
rim and femoral head-neck junction. Pincer impingement is characterized by acetabular-
based disorders, such as focal anterior over-coverage, acetabular retroversion, and
global over-coverage that create abnormal abutment of the acetabular rim and femoral
head-neck junction. Although cam and pincer impingement can occur in isolation,
combined cam/pincer deformities are thought to be most common, representing as
many as 85% of cases.
Epidemiology
Morphologic changes associated with FAI syndrome are highly prevalent in the general
population, and individuals with these changes are often asymptomatic.
Pincer impingement typically affects middle-aged females, whereas cam impingement typically
arises in younger males.
In a large multicenter study, the mean age at the time of surgery was 28 years with slight
female predominance (55%).
Impingement findings are particularly prevalent among high-level athletes.

Epidemiology
Although cam and/or pincer deformities are a necessary condition for FAI syndrome,
they frequently are encountered in asymptomatic individuals. A study of 4,151 hips in
the Copenhagen osteoarthritis study revealed cam morphology in 17% of male hips and
4% of female hips.3 This study used AP radiographs, which are not the most sensitive
imaging study for assessing cam morphology; therefore, the true incidence likely is
higher. In a study of 100 patients without a history of hip complaints, CT revealed cam
deformity in 31% of the patients (37% of males and 25% of females).4
Pincer morphology typically arises in middle-aged females (mean age, 40 years). Cam
morphology typically arises in younger patients (mean age, 32 years), with a 3:1 male to
female ratio.5 One theory posits that the male predominance of cam morphology relates
to the earlier closure of the proximal physis among females. In males, the development
and growth of cam morphology arises at a time of rapid growth (ages 12 to 16 years), at
which time many young male athletes are involved in high-intensity sports (eg, football,
hockey, basketball, and soccer).6 Men also are more likely to exhibit bilateral findings of
FAI syndrome for cam-type deformity (25% versus 6%) and pincer-type deformity (22%
versus 10%) compared with women.7 A multicenter study of 1,130 hip arthroscopy
procedures reported a mean age at surgery of 28 years, with a slight female
predominance (55% female).8
Cam impingement is particularly prevalent among high-level athletes. A study evaluating
radiographs of 239 hips at the 2009 and 2010 National Football League Scouting
Combine revealed at least one radiographic finding of FAI syndrome in 87% of the hips
(only 31% were symptomatic).9 Similarly, a study of 137 elite ice hockey players revealed
cam morphology on 70% of radiographs obtained during preseason entrance
examinations.10
Etiology

Genetic factors play an important role in the development of cam FAI syndrome. Cam
morphology is more prevalent among males, among individuals who have siblings that are
affected, and among Caucasians when compared with east Asians.
FAI syndrome frequently is observed in athletes, particularly those who participate in sports
that demand extremes of hip motion, such as gymnastics, dance, hockey, soccer, and
basketball.
Cam impingement also may arise as sequalae of pediatric hip disease, such as slipped capital
femoral epiphysis (SCFE) and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD), or as a result of femoral neck
malunion.

Etiology
The precise etiology of FAI syndrome remains unclear; however, several theories suggest
genetic factors, high-intensity athletic activity during development, pediatric deformity,
and trauma. Pollard et al11 reported that siblings of patients with FAI syndrome had a
relative risk of 2.8 and 2.0 of developing cam and pincer impingement, respectively,
compared with controls. Studies on the etiology of hip osteoarthritis in east Asian
populations have reported a very low incidence of radiographic impingement findings,
with most cases of osteoarthritis attributed to hip dysplasia.12,13 The increased
prevalence of cam impingement among males, among siblings of those with cam
impingement, and among Caucasians suggests that intrinsic genetic factors influence the
development of FAI syndrome.
FAI syndrome is particularly prevalent in the athletic population. A recent systematic
review of 208 male athletes (300 hips) determined that cam morphology was
considerably more likely to occur in athletes involved in high-impact sports (basketball,
hockey, and soccer) than in nonathletes (odds ratio, 1.9 to 8.0).14 Philippon et al15
evaluated 61 asymptomatic youth hockey players and demonstrated increased alpha
angles among hockey players compared with skiers and also demonstrated a greater
increase in alpha angle among more experienced hockey players, suggesting that
increased exposure to sport increases the likelihood of cam impingement. In a
prospective longitudinal study of adolescent soccer players at baseline and 2 years,
Agricola et al16 reported increased radiologic evidence of cam morphology at the 2-year

time point. Wolff’s law may explain the higher prevalence of cam impingement among
high-level impact athletes because bone adaptation is stimulated by repetitive
femoroacetabular contact during sports activity. Sports that have been commonly
implicated include ice hockey, basketball, football, soccer, martial arts, gymnastics, and
cheerleading.17,18
Although FAI syndrome commonly presents as atraumatic idiopathic pain in adulthood,
it also has been associated with pediatric hip diseases and prior trauma. SCFE deformity
has been shown to predispose patients to cam impingement in adulthood because of
anterosuperior displacement of the femoral metaphysis that occurs in the condition.
Similarly, LCPD may lead to cam FAI syndrome because of aspherical enlargement of the
femoral head (coxa magna) from a healed osteonecrotic femoral epiphysis. Although
LCPD and SCFE may result in cam impingement, LCPD also promotes extra-articular
trochanteric-pelvic impingement from coxa vara and trochanteric overgrowth. Cam
morphology also has been noted as a consequence of femoral neck malunion after
femoral neck fracture, with Mathew et al19 reporting a cam prevalence of 84% in a
cohort of 187 patients who underwent open reduction internal fixation. Finally, pincer
FAI syndrome may be a postoperative consequence of a Bernese periacetabular
osteotomy because of overcorrection of hip dysplasia.20,21
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Pincer impingement: femoroacetabular impingement secondary to a prominent anterior
acetabular rim because of focal anterior wall overgrowth, acetabular retroversion, or global
over-coverage (coxa profunda or protrusio acetabuli)
Cam impingement: femoroacetabular impingement secondary to focal prominence on the
anterolateral femoral head-neck junction

In pincer impingement, hip flexion brings the prominent acetabular rim into apposition
with the femoral neck, compressing the anterior labrum. Early in the disease process,
pincer impingement results in labral tearing; however, repetitive microtrauma to the
labrum in pincer impingement promotes bone growth at the acetabular rim, leading to
eventual labral ossification. With disease progression, persistent contact between the
posteroinferior acetabulum and the posteromedial aspect of the femoral head promotes
acetabular cartilage damage known as the contrecoup lesion.
In cam impingement, a focal prominence exists on the anterolateral or anterosuperior
head-neck junction, resulting in loss of femoral head-neck offset. The cam lesion also has
been described as a pistol grip deformity. Cam impingement is most symptomatic in hip
flexion, which causes the focal femoral head prominence to contact the transition zone
between the labrum and the acetabular cartilage, resulting in compressive and shear
stress at the chondrolabral junction. This results in chondrolabral separation and
cartilage delamination. Compared with pincer impingement, the labrum is relatively
spared. Rarely, repetitive cam impingement may result in acetabular rim stress fractures
or os acetabuli.22
Neurovascular Structures
The principal blood supply to the femoral head is the lateral epiphyseal branches of the medial
femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), which are at risk during osteoplasty of lateral/posterior cam
lesions.
Most neurologic complications of hip arthroscopy are related to traction.
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN) may be injured directly during placement of the
anterior portal.

Neurovascular Structures
Hip arthroscopy for FAI syndrome generally is a safe operation; however, surgeons must
be aware of at-risk neurovascular structures. The principal blood supply to the femoral
head is the lateral epiphyseal branches of the MFCA. The MFCA inserts on the
posterosuperior femoral neck between the 10:30-o’clock and 12-o’clock positions, just

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000588

posterior to the lateral synovial fold, and ascends on the femoral neck via a mean of four
vessels. Ninety-seven percent of the vessels are posterior to the 12-o’clock position,
suggesting femoral osteochondroplasty is safe on the anterior half of the femoral head-
neck junction (remaining anterior to the lateral synovial fold).23
Most neurologic injuries after hip arthroscopy can be attributed to traction used to
achieve joint distraction. In 2001, Sampson24 reported 20 neuropraxias in 530 cases (10
peroneal, 4 pudendal, 4 sciatic, 1 lateral femoral cutaneous, and 1 femoral/sciatic). The
author noted that all neuropraxias were associated with longer traction times.
Neuropraxias to the sciatic, femoral, and peroneal nerves are related to tension on the
nerves, whereas pudendal neuropraxias are to the result of direct compression to the
perineum by the perineal post. Therefore, surgeons typically can avoid neurologic
complications related to traction by limiting traction time to less than 2 hours, avoiding
over-distraction in patients with ligamentous laxity, and using a well-padded perineal
post or a post-free traction system.
The femoral and sciatic nerves are well away from the surgical field during hip
arthroscopy; however, the LFCN is at risk during placement of the anterior portal.
Because of the number of LFCN branches, it cannot be safely avoided by moving the
position of the portal.25 Therefore, avoiding injury to the LFCN requires meticulous
surgical technique, specifically avoiding deep laceration into the subcutaneous tissues.
Tendons
The iliopsoas tendon lies just superficial to the anteromedial hip joint capsule and may cause
symptoms as a result of iliopsoas tendinitis, internal snapping hip, or labral tears because of
iliopsoas impingement.
The iliotibial band lies just lateral to the greater trochanter and has been implicated in
trochanteric bursitis and external snapping hip.

Tendons

The iliopsoas tendon lies just superficial to the anteromedial hip joint capsule and comes
into view at the medial extent of the interportal capsulotomy. The iliopsoas tendon has
been implicated in various conditions, including hip flexor tendinitis, internal snapping
hip, and iliopsoas impingement. In internal snapping hip, snapping is caused by the
iliopsoas tendon sliding over the iliopectineal eminence or the femoral head as the hip is
brought from flexion/abduction into extension/adduction. The iliopsoas also has been
implicated in causing a distinct pattern of acetabular labral tears. Although most labral
tears in patients with FAI syndrome occur in the anterosuperior region (1-o’clock to 2-
o’clock positions), tears at a more anterior location directly beneath the ilopsoas tendon
(3-o’clock position) have been attributed to iliopsoas impingement. Most conditions
involving the iliopsoas tendon are managed nonsurgically via anti-inflammatories,
stretching, and avoidance of inciting activities; however, in recalcitrant cases of snapping
hip and labral tears at the psoas notch, arthroscopic iliopsoas tendon lengthening has
been proposed.26 Great care should be taken in considering psoas lengthening during
hip arthroscopy, particularly in patients with hip dysplasia and femoral anteversion
because the psoas is an important anterior hip stabilizer and lengthening may result in
irreversible anterior hip instability.
The iliotibial band is a thickened fascial tract with contributions from the tensor fascia
lata anteriorly and the gluteus maximus posteriorly that runs down the lateral thigh and
inserts onto the lateral proximal tibia at the Gerdy tubercle. In its course, the iliotibial
band runs directly lateral to the greater trochanter and, therefore, has been implicated
as a contributor to trochanteric bursitis and external snapping hip. Trochanteric bursitis
may coexist with FAI syndrome. Vap et al27 diagnosed chronic trochanteric bursitis in 90
of 1,278 patients (7%) who underwent hip arthroscopy for FAI syndrome. Trochanteric
bursitis was more commonly observed in females (odds ratio, 5.3) and patients older
than 30 years (odds ratio, 2.5). The authors managed chronic trochanteric bursitis via
iliotibial band lengthening and trochanteric bursectomy, reporting excellent pain relief
and results and outcome scores equivalent to patients who had primary FAI syndrome
without chronic trochanteric bursitis. In external snapping hip, snapping is caused by the
tight posterior aspect of the iliotibial band sliding over the greater trochanter during hip
flexion and adduction. Although internal snapping hip often is described as snapping
you can hear, external snapping hip is snapping you can see. Surgeons must ask patients

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients with FAI syndrome most commonly present with insidious hip pain localized to the
groin or C-sign distribution worsened with activity or hip hyperflexion and rotational
maneuvers.
Physical examination findings consistent with FAI syndrome include a positive impingement
test (flexion, adduction, and internal rotation test) and restricted internal rotation.
Several extra-articular hip disorders, including iliopsoas impingement, subspine impingement,
ischiofemoral impingement, trochanteric-pelvic impingement, and athletic pubalgia, can be
differentiated from FAI syndrome via a careful physical examination.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Patients with symptomatic FAI syndrome frequently present with activity-related hip pain
localized to the groin or C-sign distribution. Symptoms typically are exacerbated by hip
flexion activities (eg, prolonged sitting, squatting, car rides, donning/doffing shoes).
Patients generally report an insidious onset of symptoms; most patients do not recall a
specific injury. Audible clicking and popping is common and often is worsened with
pivoting and turning toward the affected side. Pain can radiate down the thigh or to the
medial knee (obturator nerve distribution); however, pain typically does not radiate
beyond the knee. Patients should be asked about a history of childhood hip disease,
including dysplasia, SCFE, or LCPD. Assessment of the patient’s activity level and goals of
treatment also is important.
Guided by a thorough patient history, the physical examination allows the surgeon to
differentiate between intra-articular and extra-articular sources of pain and is essential
for medical decision making. The most sensitive physical examination test for FAI
syndrome is the impingement test (88% sensitive). The impingement test is performed

by passively flexing the hip to 90° with adduction and internal rotation. The test is
positive if the patient’s symptoms are reproduced with passive hip flexion, adduction,
and internal rotation. Patients with FAI syndrome also demonstrate reduced passive
internal rotation. A study by Wyss et al28 demonstrated an inverse relationship between
the degree of passive internal rotation and cam lesion size. Posterior rim impingement is
assessed by extending the hip in an abducted and externally rotated position (hanging
the affected leg off the examination table). Reproduction of pain with passive flexion and
extension while in this position suggests a positive test. The flexion, abduction, and
external rotation test is a nonspecific maneuver that may be positive in patients with a
number of conditions, depending on the location of pain provocation. Although the
flexion, abduction, and external rotation test was traditionally used to elicit sacroiliac
joint pain (with reproduction of posterior pain), it also may be suggestive of an irritable
hip because of FAI syndrome or psoas irritation (if localized to the groin) or suggestive of
greater trochanteric pain syndrome (if localized to the lateral hip).
Several extra-articular conditions share clinical features of FAI but can be distinguished
via specific physical examination maneuvers. Iliopsoas impingement often is associated
with anterior labral tears and is heralded by pain with resisted straight leg raise or a
positive flexion, adduction, and internal rotation test. Internal snapping hip is elicited by
placing the hip in abduction and flexion and bringing it into adduction and extension; a
loud clunk often is heard or felt. Subspine impingement is caused by abutment of a
prominent anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) on the distal femoral neck.29 The subspine
impingement test is positive if pain is reproduced via maximal hip flexion in neutral
rotation and adduction. Ischiofemoral impingement is posterior hip pain caused by
abutment of the lesser trochanter with the ischial tuberosity, resulting in impingement
of the quadratus femoris muscle. The long stride walking test is positive for
ischiofemoral impingement if symptoms are exacerbated by walking quickly with a
lengthened stride but alleviated with a slower gait. The ischiofemoral impingement test
involves placing the patient in the lateral decubitus position and bringing the involved
hip from flexion to extension in abduction and adduction. Reproduction of the
symptoms with hip extension in adduction is suggestive of ischiofemoral impingement.
Trochanteric-pelvic impingement results from abutment of the greater trochanter on the
ilium as the hip moves into abduction and extension. This is most commonly observed in
patients with LCPD that result in shortening of the femoral neck, coxa vara, and greater

impingement if pain is reproduced via passive abduction and extension of the hip with
the patient in the lateral decubitus position. Core muscle injury (or althetic pubalgia) is
diagnosed on physical examination, with tenderness present over the pubic ramus at
the insertion of the rectus abdominus, pain with resisted hip adduction, or pain with
resisted sit-up.
The anterior apprehension test is indicative of hip microinstability and often is positive in
patients with dysplasia or considerable joint laxity. The patient is positioned at the end of
the examination table, and the examiner extends and externally rotates the extremity.
Anterior hip pain is consistent with an anterior labral tear and/or anterior hip instability.
This test may be particularly valuable in patients with borderline dysplasia and a positive
impingement test to differentiate FAI syndrome from dysplasia. Hypermobility of the
joints (thumb, forearm, elbow, shoulder, and knee) should be assessed if concern for
connective tissue disorder exits, and the Beighton score should be recorded. The dial
test, used to evaluate for capsular laxity or iatrogenic capsular insufficiency, is
performed with the patient in the supine position and by internally rotating the hip and
releasing the limb to allow it to rotate externally. The dial test is positive if external
rotation beyond 45° without a definitive end point is noted. Recognizing hypermobility or
capsular laxity is essential before surgical management of FAI syndrome because
capsular closure and/or plication is essential to achieving a favorable outcome in these
patients.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiography is the most important imaging modality and should include an AP pelvis
view, lateral view of the femur, and lateral view of the acetabulum.
Magnetic resonance arthrography (MRA) is the most sensitive imaging modality for the
detection of acetabular labral tears and articular cartilage lesions.
CT with three-dimensional reformatting may be useful for preoperative osteoplasty planning,
particularly in patients with complicated or subspinous deformity and for assessing the extent
of dysplasia.

Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs should include a standing AP pelvis view, a lateral view of the femur
(typically 45° Dunn view), and a lateral view of the acetabulum (false-profile view). The AP
pelvis view is used to assess acetabular anatomy, including acetabular coverage and
version, and femoral head sphericity. Global over-coverage can be characterized as coxa
profunda (floor of the acetabular fossa extends medial to the ilioischial line) or protrusio
acetabuli (femoral head extends medial to the ilioischial line). Acetabular coverage also
can be quantified on an AP radiograph using the lateral center edge angle (LCEA). The
LCEA is measured on an AP radiograph as the angle between a vertical line upward from
the center of the femoral head and a line from the center of the femoral head to the
lateral margin of the sourcil. A normal LCEA is between 25° and 40°, with measurements
greater than 40° suggestive of acetabular over-coverage and measurements less than
25° suggestive of borderline dysplasia (20° to 25°) or dysplasia (<20°). The Tönnis angle
(or acetabular index) also can be used to quantify acetabular coverage. The Tönnis angle
is the angle between a line from the medial aspect of the sourcil to the lateral aspect of
the sourcil and a horizontal line. A normal Tönnis angle is between 0° and 10°, with a
Tonnis angle less than 0° consistent with over-coverage and a Tönnis angle greater than
10° consistent with dysplasia. A positive crossover sign is indicative of cranial
retroversion and is observed if the anterior wall crosses over the posterior wall medial to
the lateral edge of the acetabulum. Signs of more global acetabular retroversion include
a positive posterior wall sign (the posterior wall is medial to the center of the femoral
head) and a positive ischial spine sine (the ischial spine is visible medial to the
iliopectineal line). The AP radiograph also is used to assess the extent of osteoarthritis
via the Tönnis classification. The Tönnis classification has important prognostic value for
patients undergoing hip arthroscopy. Hip arthroscopy is most predictable in patients
with Tönnis grade 0 or grade 1. Byrd et al30 showed progressive reductions in
improvement in modified Harris hip scores and return to sports activity with increasing
Tönnis grade (Table 1).

The false-profile view is useful to assess anterior acetabular coverage, AIIS morphology
(to assess for subspinous impingement), and posterior joint space width. Anterior
acetabular coverage is assessed via the anterior center edge angle. This is measured via
the same method as that for the LCEA but on a false-profile radiograph. Thresholds for
dysplasia, borderline dysplasia, and over-coverage are the same as those for the LCEA.
AIIS morphology can be classified as type I (smooth with no prominence between the
AIIS and acetabular rim), type II (convexity extending from the lower AIIS to the
acetabular rim), and type III (downward spur-like prominence extending below the
acetabular rim). Posterior joint space width may be narrowed in patients with early
osteoarthritis, particularly in those with pincer impingement (contrecoup lesion).
MRI or MRA are essential imaging modalities in the workup of FAI syndrome. MRI
provides information regarding the integrity of the acetabular labrum, articular cartilage,
and subchondral bone; allows for cross-sectional evaluation of cam and pincer

deformity; and allows for measurement of acetabular and femoral version. Labral tears
may appear as chondrolabral separation, partial and complete undersurface tears,
intrasubstance tears, or complex multidirectional tears. A recent prospective study
demonstrated the superiority of MRA versus non-contrast MRI with regard to the
detection of labral tears and partial-thickness acetabular cartilage lesions compared with
intraoperative findings. The sensitivity for recognition of labral tears was 81% and 69%
with MRA and 50% and 50% for two different readers. The sensitivity for identification of
articular cartilage lesions was 71% and 92% for MRA compared with 58% and 83% for
MRI. Radial sequences around the axis of the femoral neck are associated with excellent
sensitivity in identification of cam morphology. Saito et al32 reported that radial MRI
slices often identified an elevated alpha angle that was not appreciated on AP and cross-
table radiographs. Acetabular version can be assessed in the axial plane on MRI/MRA;
however, version calculations are highly dependent on the cranial-caudal level of the
slice, with more cranial levels suggesting lesser degrees of anteversion. Femoral version
also can be calculated but requires a protocol that includes axial slices of the knee to
provide the posterior condylar axis as a reference.
Although used much less broadly than plain radiographs and MRI, low-dose CT with
three-dimensional reformatting may be useful in surgical planning for patients with
complex or borderline deformities, evaluating AIIS morphology, and assessing
acetabular and femoral version. Complex deformities of the hip, such as sequelae of
LCPD, SCFE; proximal femoral deficiency; or torsional alterations of the femur require a
more detailed preoperative assessment to better understand the dynamic
pathoanatomy. CT-based image-guiding software tools are available that allow surgeons
to determine the effects of virtual osteoplasty on hip range of motion.33

Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for anterior hip pain is broad, and differentiating among
conditions requires a careful patient history and physical examination, plain radiographs
and MRIs, and diagnostic injections. A recent systematic review reported that the most
common causes of hip-related pain in athletes included FAI syndrome (32%), athletic
pubalgia (24%), adductor-related pathology (12%), and inguinal pathology (10%).34 Hip
dysplasia is the second most common source of nonarthritic hip joint pain (after FAI
syndrome) and frequently coexists with cam impingement. Although patients with FAI
syndrome typically report pain with flexion activities (prolonged sitting, donning/doffing
shoes, and ascending stairs), patients with dysplasia often report pain with prolonged
standing and walking and a sense of instability. On physical examination, patients with
dysplasia often demonstrate globally increased motion and a positive anterior
apprehension sign. On imaging studies, patients with dysplasia have a center edge angle
of less than 20° (or between 20° and 25° in borderline cases), a Tönnis angle of greater
than 10°, and MRI evidence of a hypertrophic acetabular labrum. Patients with psoas
tendon disorders, including psoas impingement, hip flexor strain, psoas tendinitis, and
internal snapping hip, present with pain with active hip flexion and often have a positive
resisted straight leg raise. Because these patients often have a positive impingement
maneuver, differential injections into the hip joint and psoas sheath may be helpful in
distinguishing these conditions. Core muscle injury (formerly athletic pubalgia or sports
hernia) is a disorder of chronic groin pain in athletes that is worsened with changes in
direction and twisting maneuvers. Patients with core muscle injury often have discrete
tenderness to the rectus abdominis insertion or the pubic symphysis, pain with a
resisted sit-up, and findings of a cleft sign on a pelvic MRI. Adductor strain is an acute
injury to the adductor longus, brevis, and/or magnus muscles and often is sporting-

Natural History
Cam FAI syndrome has been shown to contribute to osteoarthritis.
Pincer FAI syndrome does not appear to be an independent risk factor for osteoarthritis.
A joint space width of less than 2 mm is a relative contraindication to hip arthroscopy because
the risk of progression to total hip arthroplasty (THA) is quite high.
Chondral lesions observed at time of arthroscopy drastically increase the likelihood of
progression to THA.

Natural History
Based on observations of patterns of cartilage injury at the time of open surgical hip
dislocation, Ganz et al2 proposed that FAI syndrome is a precursor to osteoarthritis. This
theory has been supported by several natural history studies. A prospective study of
Dutch patients demonstrated that moderate (alpha angle >60°) and severe (alpha angle
>83°) cam deformities were associated with a 3.7- and 10-fold increased risk for
osteoarthritis relative to controls.35 The study also reported that cam morphology and a
positive impingement sign were associated with a positive predictive value of 53% for the
future development of osteoarthritis. A study on the prevalence of FAI syndrome
morphology in patients undergoing THA for osteoarthritis reported that patients
younger than 65 years were more likely to have evidence of cam lesions but not pincer
lesions.36

FAI syndrome, and normal morphology demonstrated the most rapid progression
among individuals with dysplasia, followed by FAI syndrome, followed by normal
morphology.37 Given the clear link between cam impingement and the development of

Associated Conditions
Since the recognition of FAI syndrome as a clinical entity, FAI syndrome has been
increasingly associated with other extra-articular hip pathologies. The link between FAI
syndrome and extra-articular pathology typically is rationalized via the kinetic chain

to many sources of shoulder pain in throwing athletes, limited internal rotation of the
hip joint is theorized to alter the kinetic motion of adjacent joints and soft-tissue
structures of the hip and pelvis.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
A trial of nonsurgical treatment is warranted in all patients with FAI syndrome. The decision to
proceed with surgical management for FAI syndrome is predicated on failed nonsurgical
management.
Corticosteroid injections are helpful diagnostically; however, in most patients, relief is very
short-lived.
More favorable outcomes have been reported with hip arthroscopy compared with physical
therapy.
Earlier surgical treatment should be considered in patients with larger cam lesions (alpha
angle >65°).

Surgical Management
General Principles
The surgical management of FAI syndrome has evolved rapidly and most commonly includes
hip arthroscopy or surgical hip dislocation. Periacetabular osteotomy (correcting acetabular
retroversion) and proximal femoral osteotomy (correcting femoral retroversion) are less
common procedures for FAI syndrome.
Surgical treatment varies based on patient anatomy and dynamic intraoperative examination.
Surgical management may include labral repair or débridement (the acetabular labrum is
important for maintaining the labral suction seal), acetabular rim trimming, or femoral head-
neck junction osteoplasty (the risk for femoral neck fracture increases if osteoplasty exceeds
30% of the femoral neck diameter).

clinical and radiologic evidence of FAI syndrome and/or acetabular labral tears.

dislocation revealed that hip arthroscopy resulted in better postoperative Nonarthritic

Contraindications
Advanced hip osteoarthritis is an absolute contraindication to hip arthroscopy given the
universally poor results reported in the literature. A joint space of less than 2 mm or
more than 50% joint space narrowing observed on plain radiographs is associated with
inferior outcomes and a higher rate of conversion to total hip arthroplasty.51 Hip
arthroscopy should not be performed in isolation in patients with acetabular dysplasia.
Dysplastic features, such as femoral head migration (>1 cm lateral or break in the
Shenton line) indicate more substantial instability that is not amenable to isolated hip
arthroscopy. Additional radiographic measurements that suggest acetabular dysplastic
features include an LCEA less than 20°, a Tönnis angle greater than 15°, and an anterior
center edge angle less than 20°. Periacetabular osteotomy should be considered in
patients who demonstrate this instability. Finally, anterior rim resection should be
avoided in patients with severe acetabular retroversion because it may exacerbate
instability from a posteriorly deficient acetabulum. An anteverting periacetabular
osteotomy is indicated in these patients; however, hip arthroscopy may be used as an
adjunct to pelvic or femoral osteotomy to manage intra-articular pathology. Hip
arthroscopy should not be the primary treatment option for severe patterns of FAI, such
as SCFE or LCPD deformities, because these are better managed via open surgical hip
dislocation.

surfaces and avoid iatrogenic chondral injury. Hip arthroscopy can be performed on a
standard fracture table or any other surgical table capable of achieving this distraction.
The patient is secured with the ipsilateral arm padded and folded over the chest. The
feet are secured with the use of well-padded boots. An extra-wide perineal post should
be used to minimize the risk of pudendal nerve compression and perineal skin trauma.

concern for perineal injury and improves the ease of adduction/internal rotation during
femoral osteoplasty.

modified mid-anterior portal. First, the anterolateral portal is established at the
intersection of the anterior and superior borders of the greater trochanter. The hip is

Distraction-related injuries include pudendal nerve and perineal compression injuries, femoral

Complications
A systematic review of 68 studies on hip arthroscopy in more than 7,000 patients
revealed a complication rate of 1.9%.60 The most common complications were
neurologic complications (53%), heterotopic ossification (24%), infection (15%), and
thromboembolic disease (7%). Most neurologic complications stem from longer duration
of traction and can be avoided by minimizing traction time and taking care with portal
placement (Table 2). The LFCN is the nerve most at risk for injury via direct trauma
during portal placement (Table 2). Risk factors for heterotopic ossification include male
sex, mixed impingement that requires rim trimming and femoral osteoplasty, large-
volume cam resection, and unrepaired capsulotomy. A randomized controlled trial
showed that 500 mg of naproxen twice daily reduced the rate of heterotopic ossification
to 4% compared with 46% in controls.61 Femoral neck fracture is a rare but disastrous
complication of hip arthroscopy, with Horner et al62 reporting femoral neck fracture in
43 of more than31,000 hip arthroscopy procedures (approximately 0.1%). Femoral neck
fracture results from excessive femoroplasty, and biomechanical studies suggest
increased safety if femoroplasty is limited to less than 35% of femoral neck length and
less than 4-mm depth of resection. Osteonecrosis may result from direct trauma to the
lateral epiphyseal branches of the MFCA or excessive traction. Visualization of the lateral
synovial fold during femoroplasty and restricting femoroplasty to the anterior half of the
femoral head are recommended to limit the risk of vascular injury.

Results depend on the underlying diagnosis and the condition of the articular cartilage.

disease; however, small grade IV lesions managed via microfracture do not appear to

Hip arthroscopy is associated with favorable outcomes in 70% to 90% of patients.
Positive outcomes are more likely in patients with a younger age, a male sex, a lower

labral débridement compared with labral repair. The merits of surgical management
over physical therapy have been broadly evaluated in the literature. A multicenter
randomized controlled trial of more than 600 patients with FAI syndrome (mean age, 35
years) reported considerably better International Hip Outcome Tool scores in the
surgical cohort at final follow-up.65 The efficacy of hip arthroscopy of FAI syndrome is
based on pathology and joint integrity, and chronologic age is not a contraindication. A
randomized controlled trial comparing hip arthroscopy and physical therapy among 72
patients with FAI syndrome who were aged 40 years or older reported significantly
better outcomes in the hip arthroscopy cohort with regard to modified Harris hip scores,
lower extremity functional scale scores, Hip Outcome Score activities of daily living
scores, and Hip Outcome Score sport-specific subscale scores. The most improvement
after hip arthroscopy occurs within 3 months postoperatively; however, certain
outcomes, including return to sports activity, quality of life, and pain, may improve for as
long as 2 years postoperatively.66 The results of hip arthroscopy are particularly
favorable among athletes. Compared with nonathletes, competitive athletes are more
likely to achieve a minimal clinically important difference and demonstrate substantially
higher patient-reported outcomes at 2 years postoperatvely.67 A systematic review of

returned to preseason or regular season game play after hip arthroscopy.69 A systematic
review of more than 7,000 hip arthroscopy procedures reported revision surgery in 9.5%
of patients and conversion to arthroplasty in 6.3% of patients.60 Common technical
